framework.name: SOC 2
framework.blurb: Trust Services Criteria (2017, revised 2022) — the full mandatory Common Criteria (Security) series plus Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity and Privacy, across control environment, communication, risk assessment, monitoring, control activities, access controls, system operations, change management and the four optional categories. The certification US and global enterprise buyers require before signing SaaS contracts.

CC1.1.how: Establish a code of conduct or ethics policy communicated to all staff, and back it with visible management commitment — tone from the top matters more to an auditor than the document itself, so keep evidence of leadership actually reinforcing it (a town hall mention, inclusion in onboarding).
CC1.1.evidence: The code of conduct, acknowledgement records, and evidence of leadership communication reinforcing it.

CC1.2.how: Establish independent oversight of the control environment appropriate to your size — a board with genuine independence for larger organisations, or at minimum a designated person outside day-to-day operations (an advisor, a non-executive) with visibility into security and control matters for a smaller one.
CC1.2.evidence: Board or oversight meeting minutes showing security/control matters were reviewed.

CC1.3.how: Document your management structure and reporting lines clearly enough that an auditor (and a new employee) can tell who's accountable for what — an org chart with named roles, kept current, is usually sufficient.
CC1.3.evidence: The current org chart or reporting-lines document.

CC1.4.how: Demonstrate a genuine commitment to staff competence — role-appropriate training, a defined skills expectation for security-sensitive roles, and professional development tracked rather than assumed. Attack Simulation Training results are useful supporting evidence for the security-awareness slice of this.
CC1.4.evidence: Training records aligned to role requirements, and competence assessment evidence for security-sensitive roles.

CC1.5.how: Hold individuals accountable for their assigned internal control responsibilities — performance expectations that reference control ownership, and a consequence (documented, even if informal for a small team) when a control owner doesn't meet their responsibility.
CC1.5.evidence: Role descriptions or performance documentation referencing specific control accountability.

CC2.1.how: Communicate internal control information to the people who need it — control owners should know what they're responsible for, and there should be a defined channel for control-related questions or issues to be raised, not just a policy document sitting on a shared drive.
CC2.1.evidence: Evidence of control-information communication (a wiki, an internal briefing, an onboarding module for control owners).

CC2.2.how: Communicate security objectives and individual responsibilities clearly at onboarding and whenever they change — this overlaps with A.5.4/A.6.2 above, and the same evidence generally satisfies both.
CC2.2.evidence: Onboarding materials or policy communications covering security objectives and responsibilities.

CC2.3.how: Communicate with external parties (customers, regulators, auditors) about security matters through a defined channel — a security.txt file or dedicated security contact address, a documented incident-notification process for affected customers, and a clear point of contact for an auditor's questions.
CC2.3.evidence: The published external security contact channel and evidence it's been used (an inbound security report, an auditor query response).

CC3.1.how: Set explicit risk assessment objectives — what you're trying to identify and why — before running a risk assessment, so the exercise produces comparable, useful results year over year rather than an ad hoc list. Checkpoint's own risk register and posture scan give you a running input to this.
CC3.1.evidence: A documented risk assessment methodology or objectives statement, referenced by the actual risk register.

CC3.2.how: Run a risk identification and analysis exercise at least annually, scoring likelihood and impact consistently — Checkpoint's own risk register uses exactly this model, so a scan-driven finding that gets approved into the register is direct evidence this control operates continuously, not just once a year.
CC3.2.evidence: The current risk register with likelihood/impact scoring, and evidence of at least annual review.

CC3.3.how: Explicitly consider fraud risk as part of your risk assessment — financial process manipulation, credential theft leading to payment fraud, insider risk — rather than only assessing technical/availability risks. A short fraud-risk section in your risk assessment methodology is usually enough for an SME.
CC3.3.evidence: Risk register entries or a risk assessment section specifically addressing fraud scenarios.

CC3.4.how: Reassess risk when something material changes — a new system, a new regulatory requirement, a significant staffing change — rather than only at the annual review. Tie this to your change management process (A.8.32) so a significant change automatically triggers a risk look-back.
CC3.4.evidence: Risk register updates timestamped to specific organisational or system changes.

CC4.1.how: Monitor whether your controls are actually operating as designed, not just that they exist on paper — a periodic control self-assessment, an internal audit programme, or ongoing evidence review (Checkpoint's own evidence-coverage tracking on the SoA is a running input to this) all count as monitoring activity.
CC4.1.evidence: Control monitoring/self-assessment records, or internal audit findings, showing controls were actually tested.

CC4.2.how: Have a defined path for internal control deficiencies to reach the people who can fix them — a finding from a self-assessment, an audit, or a scan shouldn't dead-end; it should land in a tracked action with an owner and a due date, exactly as Checkpoint's Actions register is designed to hold it.
CC4.2.evidence: A deficiency communicated through to a tracked remediation action, from identification to closure.

CC5.1.how: Select and design control activities that genuinely address the risks identified in your risk assessment (CC3.2) — a control that exists but doesn't map to a real risk is wasted effort, and a risk with no corresponding control is a gap worth closing.
CC5.1.evidence: A mapping (even informal) between identified risks and the controls intended to address them.

CC5.2.how: Implement technology-specific control activities — configuration baselines, patch management, access controls — consistently across your Microsoft 365 and Azure environment using Intune security baselines and documented configuration standards rather than ad hoc per-system setup.
CC5.2.evidence: Intune security baseline assignment and configuration standard documentation.

CC5.3.how: Deploy control activities through actual policies and procedures that staff can reference — not just technical configuration with no documented rationale — so a new team member or an auditor can understand why a control exists, not just that it does.
CC5.3.evidence: Policies/procedures documenting the rationale for key control activities.

CC6.1.how: Implement logical access security consistently across infrastructure and applications — Entra ID as the central identity provider, MFA enforced for everyone, and access reviewed regularly. This is the same foundational control ISO 27001's A.5.15 addresses, and the two share evidence directly.
CC6.1.evidence: The Conditional Access policy set, access-review records, and Checkpoint's mfa-all scan result.

CC6.2.how: Validate identity and authorise access before issuing system credentials — a documented new-hire access request and approval step, tied to HR onboarding, rather than IT provisioning access on an informal request.
CC6.2.evidence: New-account provisioning records showing approval before credential issuance.

CC6.3.how: Remove access promptly on role change or termination — an offboarding/role-change checklist tied to HR events, with same-day Entra account disablement for terminations. This is the same control ISO 27001's A.6.5 addresses.
CC6.3.evidence: Offboarding/role-change records matched against Entra account modification timestamps.

CC6.4.how: Restrict physical access to facilities holding sensitive systems or information, appropriate to your environment — see the equivalent ISO 27001 A.7.1-A.7.2 guidance, which applies identically here.
CC6.4.evidence: A physical access log or the documented rationale where a physical perimeter doesn't apply.

CC6.5.how: Discontinue both physical and logical access together on termination — a departing employee's building access, VPN, and Entra account should all be revoked as part of the same offboarding action, not handled by three different people on three different days.
CC6.5.evidence: A unified offboarding checklist covering physical and logical access, completed for a sample of recent departures.

CC6.6.how: Protect logical access boundaries — Conditional Access enforcing device compliance and location-based restrictions, network segmentation for anything hosted in Azure — so a compromised credential alone isn't enough to reach sensitive systems.
CC6.6.evidence: The Conditional Access policy set enforcing boundary conditions, and network segmentation configuration where applicable.

CC6.7.how: Restrict how data moves and is transmitted — encryption in transit by default (Microsoft 365 does this natively for most traffic), DLP policies controlling what leaves the tenant, and Conditional Access restricting data access from unmanaged devices.
CC6.7.evidence: DLP policy configuration and Conditional Access restrictions on data access from unmanaged devices.

CC6.8.how: Prevent and detect malicious software — Defender's real-time protection across endpoints and email, with alerting that's actually monitored (see CC7.2/A.8.16). A control that only prevents but never detects leaves you blind to anything that gets through.
CC6.8.evidence: Defender configuration showing prevention enabled, and alert-monitoring evidence for detection, plus Checkpoint's wdac scan result.

CC7.1.how: Run vulnerability detection consistently — Microsoft Secure Score and Defender's vulnerability management surface known gaps automatically; the control is making sure someone actually reviews and actions the findings on a set cadence rather than the tooling running unattended.
CC7.1.evidence: Vulnerability scan/Secure Score review records, and Checkpoint's patch scan result.

CC7.2.how: Monitor for security events continuously, not just react when something is reported — Defender's alert queue with unified audit logging behind it, reviewed on a defined cadence with a documented escalation path for anything significant.
CC7.2.evidence: Alert monitoring/triage records and Checkpoint's logging scan result confirming audit logging is enabled.

CC7.3.how: Evaluate security incidents to determine scope and impact before deciding on a response — a brief triage assessment (what happened, what's affected, how bad) for every incident above a low severity threshold, recorded even when the conclusion is 'contained, no further action'.
CC7.3.evidence: Incident evaluation records showing scope/impact assessment for a sample of incidents.

CC7.4.how: Respond to identified security incidents through a documented process — containment, eradication, recovery — using Defender's automated investigation and response capability where licensed, and a clear escalation path to management for anything significant.
CC7.4.evidence: Incident response records showing the response process was followed, from identification to resolution.

CC7.5.how: Recover from security incidents through a documented process, including confirming the underlying cause is actually fixed before declaring the incident closed — reopening an incident because the same issue recurs is worse for an audit than taking longer to close it properly the first time.
CC7.5.evidence: Incident recovery records showing root-cause remediation confirmed before closure.

CC8.1.how: Run a documented change management process for anything affecting production systems — request, risk/impact assessment, testing, approval, and a rollback plan, proportionate to the change's risk. See the identical guidance under ISO 27001's A.8.32; the same evidence satisfies both.
CC8.1.evidence: Change records for a sample of recent changes showing the full approval and testing workflow.

CC9.1.how: Identify and mitigate risks that could cause a business disruption — the same continuity planning covered under ISO 27001's A.5.29/A.5.30 — with a documented business continuity plan and evidence it's been tested, not just written and filed.
CC9.1.evidence: The business continuity plan and a record of at least one test or exercise.

CC9.2.how: Manage vendor and business partner risk through a documented assessment before onboarding and periodic review afterward — Checkpoint's Vendor register with data-access classification and suggested criticality is built specifically to hold this evidence, satisfying the same control ISO 27001's A.5.19/A.5.22 address.
CC9.2.evidence: The vendor risk register with pre-onboarding assessments and periodic reviews recorded.

A1.1.how: For a Microsoft 365 tenant, capacity is mostly Microsoft's problem — what's yours is licence and quota headroom. Track mailbox and SharePoint storage consumption in the admin center reports, set alerts before site collections hit quota, and review licence utilisation quarterly so growth doesn't outrun what you've purchased. If you run Azure workloads, add Azure Monitor autoscale rules or at minimum capacity alerts on the resources that back your service commitments.
A1.1.evidence: A recurring capacity review record (storage/licence utilisation report with the date reviewed) and any configured storage or Azure Monitor alerts.

A1.2.how: Lean on the shared-responsibility model deliberately rather than by accident: document that environmental protections for Microsoft 365 data sit with Microsoft's datacenters, and attach Microsoft's SOC 2 report from the Service Trust Portal as your evidence. Your side of the control is data resilience — confirm retention policies in Purview protect against destructive loss, and cover any on-premises or Azure infrastructure you still own with its own backup and environmental story. Auditors accept inheritance here, but only if you've actually reviewed the subservice report.
A1.2.evidence: Microsoft's current SOC 2 report (downloaded from the Service Trust Portal, with your review noted) plus your own backup/retention configuration for tenant data.

A1.3.how: A recovery plan you've never exercised is what auditors call a finding. Run at least an annual test: restore a deleted SharePoint site or mailbox item from Purview retention, walk through the business continuity plan as a tabletop, and record what broke. Checkpoint's bcp check confirms a plan exists — the test record is what proves it works.
A1.3.evidence: A dated recovery test report or tabletop exercise record, including issues found and remediation actions.

C1.1.how: Define a classification scheme and implement it as Purview sensitivity labels — 'Confidential' and above should carry real protections (encryption, watermarking, or sharing restrictions), not just a coloured tag. Publish the labels to all users via a label policy, set a sensible default, and use auto-labelling for the obvious cases like credit card numbers or client identifiers. The auditor will ask how you know confidential data is actually being labelled, so keep the label usage analytics from Purview handy.
C1.1.evidence: The published sensitivity label taxonomy and policy export, plus label usage reporting showing adoption.

C1.2.how: Disposal in Microsoft 365 means retention policy expiry doing the deleting for you: configure Purview retention/deletion policies so confidential content is destroyed on schedule rather than accumulating indefinitely, and use disposition review for anything that needs a human sign-off before destruction. For hardware, Intune wipe/retire covers managed devices; document the certificate-of-destruction expectation for anything physical that leaves your hands.
C1.2.evidence: Retention policy configuration showing deletion actions, disposition review records, and device wipe logs from Intune.

PI1.1.how: Write down, per key process, what 'good' input data looks like — required fields, formats, validity ranges — and enforce it where the data enters: column validation in SharePoint lists, required fields and input validation in Power Apps forms, schema checks in Power Automate flows before data lands anywhere downstream. The definition matters as much as the enforcement; auditors ask to see the documented data quality requirements first.
PI1.1.evidence: Documented data quality requirements for in-scope processes and the validation configuration (form/flow definitions) that enforces them.

PI1.2.how: Maintain a data-flow inventory for each in-scope processing system: what inputs it accepts, from whom, in what format, and what processing objective they serve. In practice this is a documented data flow diagram plus the input specifications — for Power Platform or custom apps, the connector and trigger definitions are your source of truth. Keep it dated and re-reviewed when the system changes.
PI1.2.evidence: Current data flow documentation and input specifications for each system in the processing-integrity scope.

PI1.3.how: Build authorisation and error handling into the processing itself: Power Automate approval steps before records are committed, exception queues for failed runs, and run-history monitoring with alerts on failures rather than someone noticing weeks later. Segregate who can modify the flows/logic from who approves the transactions — Entra ID groups and environment security roles in Power Platform do this cleanly.
PI1.3.evidence: Flow/process definitions showing approval and exception handling, run-failure alert configuration, and a sample of resolved processing exceptions.

PI1.4.how: Prove outputs are complete, accurate, and delivered to the right recipients: reconciliation or record-count checks between input and output where volumes matter, and access controls on output locations so reports only reach their intended audience — SharePoint permissions scoped to the recipient group, sensitivity labels on the output files, DLP to stop them leaking further. Auditors probe the 'intended recipients' half hardest, so the access configuration on the output store is the core evidence.
PI1.4.evidence: Reconciliation/completeness check records and the permission configuration of output locations showing distribution is restricted to intended recipients.

PI1.5.how: Storage integrity is retention plus protection: Purview retention policies keep inputs and outputs for as long as the processing objectives require, versioning in SharePoint/OneDrive protects against accidental overwrite, and restricted write access stops tampering. If records must be provably unmodified, use Purview records management to declare them immutable records.
PI1.5.evidence: Retention policy configuration covering processing inputs/outputs, and versioning/records-management settings on the stores that hold them.

P1.1.how: Publish a privacy notice that describes what you actually do — collection, purposes, disclosures, retention, and how to complain — and keep it versioned so you can show what was live at any point in the audit period. Under APP 1 and APP 5 the notice must be current and available at or before collection, so link it from every collection point (web forms, onboarding packs) and diarise an annual review. Auditors compare the notice against real practice, so review it whenever processing changes, not just on the anniversary.
P1.1.evidence: The published privacy notice with version history, and records of its periodic review and approval.

P2.1.how: Map every collection point and confirm each one presents a genuine choice: unticked-by-default consent for anything beyond the core service, granular options rather than bundled consent, and the consent capture stored somewhere queryable — a Dataverse table or SharePoint list written by the intake form works fine. The failure mode auditors find is consent language that doesn't match what the systems then do with the data, so reconcile the two.
P2.1.evidence: Consent capture records (who, when, what wording, what they agreed to) and screenshots of the consent UI at collection points.

P3.1.how: Limit collection to what the notice disclosed: strip optional fields from intake forms that gather 'nice to have' data, and use Purview data classification to scan what you actually hold — sensitive info types turning up where your notice never mentioned them is exactly what this criterion is about. A periodic reconciliation of forms-versus-notice is cheap and closes the gap before an auditor does it for you.
P3.1.evidence: A collection-point inventory reconciled against the privacy notice, plus Purview data classification results for the stores involved.

P3.2.how: Sensitive information (health, biometrics, and the other APP 3 special categories) needs explicit, recorded consent — a separate affirmative step, not a line buried in general terms. Configure the collecting forms to require that distinct opt-in and store the record; then use Purview sensitive information types and auto-labelling to find and protect sensitive data wherever it lands, since discovery of unconsented sensitive data is the audit risk here.
P3.2.evidence: Explicit consent records tied to the sensitive-data collection points, and Purview classification/auto-labelling configuration for sensitive info types.

P4.1.how: Purpose limitation lives or dies on access scoping: personal information collected for purpose X shouldn't be broadly readable by teams working on purpose Y. Restrict the stores holding personal information with Entra ID groups, apply sensitivity labels that travel with the files, and use DLP to block movement into out-of-purpose locations. Document the permitted uses per data category so 'consistent with stated purposes' is testable rather than vibes.
P4.1.evidence: A data-use register mapping personal information categories to permitted purposes, and the access/DLP configuration enforcing it.

P4.2.how: Turn your retention schedule into enforced Purview retention policies with deletion actions — a schedule that exists only in a Word document while mailboxes keep everything forever is the most common gap in this criterion. Apply retention labels per record type (HR files, customer records, support tickets), set the clocks from the right trigger event, and let disposition review handle the edge cases.
P4.2.evidence: The approved retention schedule and the matching Purview retention policy/label export showing deletion is actually configured.

P4.3.how: Secure disposal of personal information: Purview retention expiry performs the deletion in Microsoft 365, disposition review gives you the auditable destruction record, and Intune wipe/retire handles managed endpoints. Don't forget the copies — backups, exports sitting in OneDrive, and third parties holding your data all need disposal covered, contractually where you don't control the systems.
P4.3.evidence: Disposition/destruction records from Purview, device wipe logs, and vendor disposal attestations where third parties hold the data.

P5.1.how: Stand up a working access-and-correction channel: a published request route (the privacy notice should point at it), an intake queue — a shared mailbox or Forms-to-Planner flow is enough — and Purview eDiscovery or Content search to actually locate an individual's information across Exchange, SharePoint, OneDrive and Teams when a request lands. APP 12 and APP 13 set the baseline: respond within a reasonable period (30 days is the OAIC's benchmark), and record the correction made.
P5.1.evidence: The documented request procedure and a log of access/correction requests showing receipt dates, searches run, and responses within the defined timeframe.

P5.2.how: When you deny an access or correction request, APP 12/13 require written reasons and a path to complain — so template the denial letter now: the ground relied on, the individual's right to complain internally and then to the OAIC, and (for corrections) their right to have a statement attached to the record. Track denials in the same request log so the pattern is reviewable.
P5.2.evidence: Denial correspondence showing reasons and recourse information, recorded in the access-request log.

P6.1.how: Control the disclosure paths, not just the policy: Purview DLP blocking personal information from leaving via email or Teams to unauthorised domains, SharePoint external sharing restricted to allowlisted partners, and Entra guest access reviewed so third-party visibility matches current agreements. Maintain the authoritative list of permitted recipients and the basis for each — every disclosure route in the tenant should trace back to it.
P6.1.evidence: The register of authorised third-party recipients and the DLP/external-sharing configuration restricting disclosure to them.

P6.2.how: Keep a disclosure register: recipient, date, what personal information, and the authority for it. For systematic disclosures (integrations, scheduled exports) record the flow once and reference it; for ad-hoc disclosures make the register entry part of the release procedure. Purview audit logs of external sharing back the register up, but the register itself is the deliverable — auditors want completeness, which raw logs alone don't demonstrate.
P6.2.evidence: The disclosure register, current through the audit period, reconcilable against sharing/audit logs.

P6.3.how: Unauthorized disclosures need their own record — fold it into your incident register with fields for what personal information was involved, how the disclosure was detected (DLP alert, user report, Defender incident), affected individuals, and containment. Wire Purview DLP incident alerts and Defender alerts into the intake so detection is systematic; 'we log the breaches we happen to hear about' does not pass.
P6.3.evidence: The privacy incident/unauthorized disclosure register with detection source, scope, and response recorded for each event.

P6.4.how: Before personal information flows to any vendor, get privacy commitments in writing — a DPA or contract clauses covering permitted use, security, subcontractors, and return/destruction. Run this through the vendor register: classify each vendor by personal-information access, and make a signed agreement a gating condition before access is provisioned, not paperwork chased afterwards. Auditors sample vendors and ask for the agreement pre-dating the data flow.
P6.4.evidence: Signed DPAs/privacy clauses for each third party receiving personal information, linked from the vendor register with dates preceding data access.

P6.5.how: Check every DPA includes a breach-notification obligation running to you — a defined notification window (72 hours is the common benchmark) and enough detail to meet your own NDB scheme assessment duties. Track this as a yes/no attribute per vendor in the register so the gap analysis is one filter, and chase the legacy contracts that predate the clause.
P6.5.evidence: Vendor register showing breach-notification clauses confirmed per vendor, with the contract language for a sample.

P6.6.how: Document a breach-notification procedure aligned to the Notifiable Data Breaches scheme: the 30-day assessment of whether serious harm is likely, who decides, the OAIC notification form, and templates for notifying affected individuals. Rehearse it — a tabletop that runs a DLP alert through to a draft OAIC statement is an afternoon's work and exactly the evidence an auditor wants when there's been no real breach to point at.
P6.6.evidence: The breach response procedure, notification templates, and either real notification records or a dated tabletop exercise covering the notification decision.

P6.7.how: Be able to answer 'what do you hold about me and who have you given it to' on request. Purview Content search across workloads finds what you hold; the disclosure register from P6.2 supplies the who. Fold this into the same subject-request procedure as P5.1 so one intake handles access, correction, and accounting-of-disclosures requests with the same timeframes.
P6.7.evidence: The procedure covering accounting-of-disclosure requests and a sample response (or a documented dry run) showing holdings and disclosures reported to an individual.

P7.1.how: Accuracy is mostly process: identify the systems of record for each personal-information category, prevent stale duplicates (one authoritative list, not five exported spreadsheets — DLP and sharing restrictions help contain sprawl), and propagate corrections from P5.1 requests to every downstream copy. A periodic data-quality review of key records — even a sampled one — gives the criterion a heartbeat auditors can test.
P7.1.evidence: Documented systems of record, correction-propagation records, and periodic data-quality review results.

P8.1.how: Close the loop on the whole privacy program: a published complaints channel with an owner and response SLA, a complaints register feeding a periodic privacy compliance review, and escalation of systemic issues into corrective actions. Auditors read this criterion as 'show me the program is monitored' — a standing agenda item in a management or governance meeting, minuted, with privacy metrics (requests, complaints, incidents) does more than any policy document.
P8.1.evidence: The complaints register, response records within SLA, and minutes of periodic privacy compliance reviews showing issues tracked to closure.
